By Waqas Qureshi 14 September 2026

Recycle Week | Survey finds 1% of people never recycle, 38% could recycle more

A new survey conducted by the campaign Recycle Now has found one third of Britons acknowledge they could recycle more.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:15
Instaread
File image: Wales recycling collections (Shutterstock)

The survey was conducted to mark Recycle Week, which runs from 14 – 20 September.

It found only 1% of people never recycle.

Over one in three (38%) agree they could recycle more than they currently do.

Adam Herriott, Recycle Week spokesperson, said: “We’re a nation of recyclers, but our annual citizen tracker shows that the number of people who feel recycling is worthwhile has dropped from 81% in 2021, to 69% today.”

Recycle Week is reminding people that recycling is the unsung energy hero that can help to reduce our energy demand; for example, recycling one deodorant can save enough energy to charge a phone forty times and recycling a plastic shampoo bottle uses just 12% of the energy needed to make one from scratch.

The introduction of Simper Recycling in England from March means many more homes are receiving food waste collections for the first time. These help to capture organic material that can be recycled to generate electricity – recycling just eight banana peels generates enough energy to boil a kettle – and produces organically rich digestate for farmland.

Despite 57% of UK households questioned saying they receive food waste collections and are using them, the dominant disposal route for most items of food remains the general rubbish.

Britons aged between 18 and 34 are more likely to put every food item straight in the general rubbish rather than recycle or compost it, and anything in the packet – whether out-of-date food or half-eaten – goes straight into the bin far more often than into the food waste caddy, meaning neither food nor packaging are recycled, but incinerated or buried in landfill.

The survey found that Britons are happy to correct someone else’s recycling mistakes, and 32% of people will remove a recyclable item from the general rubbish and put it in recycling when someone else has put it in the wrong bin.

Emma Hardy, waste minister, said: “I fully support Recycle Week and its aim to help people recycle more of the right things, more often. This Recycle Week, I encourage everyone to check the Recycle Now Locator to see what can be recycled in their area and help keep more valuable materials in use for longer.”
